title: Infotainment responds immediately to touch and voice so interactions feel instantaneous
description: When the driver or passenger touches the centre screen or uses voice, the system reacts without noticeable delay so interactions feel immediate and natural (no visible lag, no spinning/loading states). This reduces frustration and makes routine tasks feel fast.
acceptance_criterion: Instrumented in-vehicle usability test: 30 participants (EU 5 Series target demographic: ages 30–70, 50% self-identified as non-technical, balanced gender, mix of current BMW owners and prospective buyers) each performs a scripted set of 20 representative touchscreen/voice actions (20 actions × 30 participants = 600 measured actions). Measure system response latency (time from user input — touch or voice command — to first visible UI response). Pass if (a) the median latency across all measured actions ≤ 120 ms, and (b) the 95th percentile latency across all measured actions ≤ 250 ms. Secondary perceptual check: at least 90% of participants must rate perceived responsiveness ≥ 4 on a 1–5 Likert scale after the session. Test runs must be performed in at least 5 vehicles (different build dates) under typical in-car conditions (ambient temp 15–25°C, normal cellular signal).

customer_pain.explanation: Mostly competitor advantages (Difficult to Use), 17 mentions

reach.explanation: 17 of at most 40 mentions (square root scale); EU = 40 % of 2030 volume (127,000 cars)

competitive_pressure.explanation: competitor advantage backed by a high-trust web source

future_relevance.explanation: no trend behind it; market growth 2025-2030: +10.4 %

rationale: Ranked mainly because of customer pain (16.9 points) and competitive pressure (15 points). Evidence level A: 17 mentions, confirmed by 3 independent source types.
assumptions: Test vehicles under test have production-level software representative of the candidate release.
Instrumentation is capable of measuring from input event to first-frame UI update with ±10 ms precision.
Typical in-car connectivity conditions are available for any cloud-backed UI actions; purely local UI actions should meet latency targets independently of network.
Tasks are implemented as they would be presented to customers in production software (no engineering-only shortcuts).
Voice invocation counts as one interaction if it completes the task without intermediate screen taps.
Driving-simulated environment is used to emulate attention constraints; non-safety-critical tasks may allow brief glances.
Driving-simulator prompts are representative of typical on-road prompts (safety-critical warnings that must be presented are excluded from suppression).
’Blocking modal’ is defined as a dialog that requires explicit user dismissal before continuing the primary driving UI.
Production-level wording and localization are used for prompts during the test.
The 2025 study questionnaire and scoring rubric are available to replicate exactly.
Sample quotas will match the original study to ensure comparability (age, country, ownership status).
Connected-services scope includes companion app flows and OTA update experience as evaluated in the original instrument.
uncertainties: Current G60 baseline latency (median and 95th percentile) is not provided in the signals; baseline measurements must be taken before A/B comparisons.
Some features (map rendering, large OTA-installed apps) may have different performance characteristics; scope here covers standard cockpit UI actions (menus, climate, media, common voice intents).
The existing G60 task interaction counts and times are not supplied in the signals; comparator baseline should be measured before formal A/B comparisons.
Some customers may prefer physical controls; this requirement targets touchscreen/voice flow efficiency, not whether physical knobs are retained.
Signals describe prompts as 'intrusive' but do not catalogue which specific dialogs trigger the most complaints; a prompt audit is required to prioritise changes.
Regulatory-required safety warnings may limit the ability to suppress certain dialogs; those exceptions will be documented and excluded from the suppression metric.
If the original 2025 study instrument or sampling frame is not available, an equivalent validated questionnaire must be produced before testing.
Some issues (e.g., app store approvals or third-party service outages) are external to vehicle software and may affect results.

offer_check.note: BMW Operating System 8.5 is the infotainment platform enabling fast touch response and integration with the voice assistant. (BMW Operating System 8.5)

title: Deliver usable electric range and consistent cold‑weather performance that meets customer expectations
description: Customers can complete typical daily trips on electric power even in cold weather and do not experience the large shortfalls vs advertised range that cause slower driving or extra charging stops. Variants that today are praised for reliable range keep that reliability across temperatures and driving styles.
acceptance_criterion: Measure electric‑only real‑world range in a standardized cold‑weather test (ambient temperature -7 ±2 °C) using N=20 production successor vehicles with 100% start SOC, standardized urban/suburban driving profile (50% city, 50% mixed speed), and no battery preconditioning. Record the distance driven until the vehicle exits electric‑only mode. Pass if (a) the fleet mean real‑world cold‑weather electric range >= 60 km, and (b) no more than 10% of tested vehicles have an individual range < 50 km. Report per‑vehicle values and full test logs. When variants today receive praise for reliable range, those variants must meet the same pass thresholds in this test.

customer_pain.explanation: Mostly complaints (Difficult to Use / Likes), 18 mentions

reach.explanation: 18 of at most 40 mentions (square root scale); EU = 40 % of 2030 volume (127,000 cars)

satisfaction_gap.explanation: Fuel economy/ energy efficiency: mean 7.45 of 10

competitive_pressure.explanation: competitor advantage backed by a high-trust web source

future_relevance.explanation: no trend behind it; market growth 2025-2030: +10.4 %

rationale: Ranked mainly because of customer pain (20.1 points) and competitive pressure (15 points). Evidence level A: 18 mentions, confirmed by 3 independent source types.
assumptions: Typical customer daily trips in target markets are adequately represented by a 50/50 city/mixed driving profile and a 60 km cold‑weather target is aligned with customer expectations for a premium PHEV sedan in 3–5 years.
Successor will offer PHEV variants aimed at providing at least this level of electric range.

The onboard estimator will have access to typical vehicle sensors and state data used today to compute range estimates; the validation focuses on end‑user accuracy rather than internal algorithm details.
In‑car UI can surface charger handshake information and estimated time‑to‑charge in route planning and during charging sessions.
User trial scenarios reflect common EU public‑charging conditions (varying charger power, congestion).
uncertainties: Current baseline cold‑weather measured range for the 2025 G60 under this exact protocol is not available and should be measured before comparative claims.
Real‑world results may vary by optional equipment (wheel size, roof load) not fully controlled in the fleet sample; test vehicles must be representative of common customer configurations.
Baseline MAPE for the current G60 under the same protocol must be measured to support relative claims; this requirement sets an absolute target for successor validation.
Actual charger handshake behaviour in the field may vary by charger operator; validation uses simulated or recorded real‑world handshake logs to ensure reproducible user trials.

offer_check.note: No listed option provides battery thermal management, heat‑pump or explicit preconditioning to ensure reliable cold‑weather range.

title: Make loading/unloading typical checked suitcases and carry‑ons quick and ergonomically easy without folding rear seats
description: When using the 5 Series luggage area, a single adult can load common checked suitcases and carry‑on bags quickly and without awkward tilting, lifting above shoulder height, or having to fold rear seats. Customers perceive loading/unloading as noticeably easier than the current model.
acceptance_criterion: Two-part validation: (1) Subjective: In a controlled EU consumer study that repeats the 2025 methodology, the mean ease‑of‑loading/unloading score increases from the G60 baseline of 7.2 (EU study 2025) to at least 8.2. Sample: 200 participants matched to the 5 Series shopper/owner demographic (age, gender, household travel behaviour). Statistical test: paired or matched sample against the G60 baseline or a matched G60 control group; result significant at p<0.05. (2) Objective task: 30 different adult participants (balanced by sex, ages 18–65, carrying typical luggage-handling strength) each perform an individual loading trial: load 3 checked suitcases (assumed dimensions 76×50×32 cm) plus 2 cabin bags (assumed dimensions 55×40×20 cm) into the luggage area without folding rear seats. Success is defined as completing the load within 90 seconds without needing two‑person assistance or forceful wedging. Pass threshold: ≥27/30 successful trials (90%). Record time, need for assistance, and any damage to luggage.

reach.explanation: 3 of at most 40 mentions (square root scale); EU = 40 % of 2030 volume (127,000 cars)

satisfaction_gap.explanation: Ease of loading/ unloading luggage: mean 7.24 of 10

competitive_pressure.explanation: competitor advantage backed by a high-trust web source

future_relevance.explanation: no trend behind it; market growth 2025-2030: +10.4 %

rationale: Ranked mainly because of customer pain (16.7 points) and competitive pressure (15 points). Evidence level C: Only 3 mentions: a hint, not a solid finding.
assumptions: Standard checked suitcase dimensions for the test are 76×50×32 cm and cabin bag dimensions 55×40×20 cm.
90 seconds is a realistic target for a single person to load this set of luggage; this target assumes the luggage aperture height, sill design and cargo floor layout allow ergonomic placement.
The EU 2025 study methodology for the subjective score is available and can be replicated for a matched sample.
uncertainties: Objective baseline measures of G60 real‑world loading success (same suitcase set and task) are not available and must be measured before final validation.
The 2025 subjective baseline (mean 7.2) must be verified to be from a comparable sample and questionnaire wording; differences in protocol could affect comparability.

title: Rear-seat occupants perceive and experience noticeably more room for long trips, including taller passengers
description: Rear passengers—especially taller adults—experience improved legroom and headroom for multi‑hour journeys: they report less leg/head discomfort and objectively have measurable knee clearance behind a typical front seat position.
acceptance_criterion: Two-part validation: (1) Subjective: Using the same EU study methodology, mean rear interior roominess score improves from the G60 baseline of 7.5 to at least 8.5. Sample: 200 participants representative of 5 Series shoppers/owners; ensure ≥30% of participants are tall (height ≥185 cm). Statistical significance p<0.05 versus baseline or matched G60 control. (2) Objective: Seating‑fit task: pairs of adults where at least one occupant is ≥185 cm sit in the rear behind a front seat set to a representative driving position for a 95th‑percentile driver. Measure knee clearance (rear occupant femur to front seat back) and head clearance. Pass if ≥80% of tested rear occupants have ≥50 mm knee clearance and no head contact at normal posture. Test sample: 30 rear occupant tests with the described height distribution and repeated on 5 vehicles (total 150 measurements).

reach.explanation: 6 of at most 40 mentions (square root scale); EU = 40 % of 2030 volume (127,000 cars)

competitive_pressure.explanation: competitor advantage backed by a medium-trust web source

future_relevance.explanation: no trend behind it; market growth 2025-2030: +10.4 %

rationale: Ranked mainly because of customer pain (14.6 points) and satisfaction gap (10.3 points). Evidence level B: Only 6 mentions, but confirmed by 2 independent source types.
assumptions: ‘Comfortable’ knee clearance is operationalised as ≥50 mm of free space in normal seating posture for sustained travel.
Front seat driving position for the 95th‑percentile driver will be defined according to an agreed EU anthropometric reference for comparability.
The EU 2025 rear‑roominess study protocol and questionnaire are reproducible for the subjective part.
uncertainties: A directly comparable objective baseline (G60 knee/head clearance measured using the exact test setup above) is not available and must be measured before final validation; Autocar’s published figure (~740 mm knee room) uses a different test method.
Passenger posture during long trips may vary; the 50 mm knee clearance assumption is a comfort threshold based on ergonomic literature but could be refined by further user testing.

offer_check.note: No listed option increases rear legroom or offers rear-seat adjustment to provide noticeably more space for taller passengers.

title: Deliver faster, more consistent cabin thermal comfort and perceived HVAC performance for all seating positions
description: Customers experience the cabin reaching a comfortable temperature quickly after startup and report consistent comfort across front and rear seats (no cold/hot spots). Perceived heating/ventilation/air conditioning performance is improved versus the current model.
acceptance_criterion: Two-part validation: (1) Subjective: In a repeat of the 2025 EU study methodology, the mean HVAC satisfaction score increases from the G60 baseline of 7.5 to at least 8.5. Sample: 200 participants matched to 5 Series shoppers/owners; statistical significance p<0.05 versus baseline or matched control. (2) Objective: Environmental‑chamber test: with vehicle cabin pre‑cooled to -10°C ambient, set climate to Auto and target 21°C. Measured at front and rear seating positions, the cabin must reach 21°C ±2°C within 8 minutes and show ≤2°C temperature variance between seating positions within 15 minutes. Test sample: 15 vehicles, 3 repeated runs each (45 runs). Pass threshold: ≥42/45 runs meet the timing and variance criteria (≥93%). Record setup, sensor locations and repeatability.

reach.explanation: 2 of at most 40 mentions (square root scale); EU = 40 % of 2030 volume (127,000 cars)

satisfaction_gap.explanation: Heating/ ventilation/ air conditioning: mean 7.47 of 10

competitive_pressure.explanation: competitor advantage backed by a medium-trust web source

future_relevance.explanation: no trend behind it; market growth 2025-2030: +10.4 %

rationale: Ranked mainly because of customer pain (18.8 points) and satisfaction gap (10.2 points). Evidence level C: Only 2 mentions: a hint, not a solid finding.
assumptions: Comfort target is defined as 21°C cabin air temperature; ±2°C is considered perceivably consistent across seats for typical occupants.
8 minutes to reach target from -10°C is a realistic and customer‑meaningful improvement target for a successor model.
The EU 2025 HVAC satisfaction study protocol is reproducible for the subjective part.
uncertainties: Objective baseline metrics for G60 time‑to‑temperature and inter-seat variance under the exact chamber protocol above are not available and must be measured before final validation.

The Mercedes‑E‑Class signal highlights competitor comfort positioning (softer ride) rather than direct HVAC metrics; using it assumes customers link overall perceived cabin comfort to HVAC responsiveness.

title: Keep the car's engaging, quiet and comfortable driving feel
description: Drivers experience the successor 5 Series as at least as fun, refined and comfortable to drive as the current G60: strong, quiet acceleration, confident handling, and well‑positioned, intuitive controls across everyday and touring routes.
acceptance_criterion: Conduct a blinded on‑road comparative driving study with N=30 licensed drivers (balanced by age 25–65 and gender, mixed urban/suburban/touring driving experience). Each driver completes the same 60 km route in the baseline G60 (model year 2025) and the successor car, in randomized order, with matched tire type and load. After each drive, drivers rate 'Overall Driving Experience' on a 1–10 scale and answer a 5‑question usability checklist about control placement. Pass if (a) the successor's mean Overall Driving Experience rating is >= the baseline G60 mean (baseline mean must be measured before validation) and (b) at least 80% of drivers give 'acceptable' or better responses on the usability checklist for the successor. Record and report per‑driver results; report fails if more than 1 vehicle shows a systematic negative outlier (>=1.5 points lower than baseline mean).

title: Use emerging high‑power public charging to materially shorten long‑distance charging stops (assumes broad HVC adoption)
description: When customers connect at modern high‑power public chargers available on main corridors, they experience significantly shorter 20–80% charging times compared with current HPC averages and the car reports realistic timelines to the driver.
acceptance_criterion: Field trial across N=20 high‑power public charging sessions at CCS‑compatible sites (minimum available peak power 300 kW at the pedestal) in representative EU locations. For each session record peak sustained power and the elapsed time from 20% to 80% SOC. Pass if the median 20–80% time across sessions is <= 15 minutes and at least 70% of sessions achieve a measured peak power >= 200 kW. Also, the vehicle's predicted 20–80% time at session start must be within ±20% of the measured time in at least 80% of sessions. Participants and sessions should reflect typical customer usage (loaded vehicle, ambient temperature logged).

reach.explanation: 2 of at most 40 mentions (square root scale); EU = 40 % of 2030 volume (127,000 cars)

competitive_pressure.explanation: no trusted web source shows a competitor advantage

future_relevance.explanation: linked to a 3-5 year trend (assumption); market growth 2025-2030: +10.4 %

rationale: Ranked mainly because of future relevance (10 points) and customer pain (7.5 points). Evidence level D: Bet on the next generation: only 0 direct customer mentions, the rest rests on trends (assumption).
assumptions: Public high‑power charging infrastructure (modular HYC1000‑class or comparable CCS pedestals) is installed and accessible to non‑Tesla premium vehicles at the time of successor launch.
Successor battery chemistry and thermal management support high‑power charging without premature tapering to very low power.
Charge station operators provide at least some pedestals capable of sustained >=300 kW power and support for the connector standard used in the EU.
uncertainties: Availability of compatible high‑power pedestals at enough geographic locations for a 20‑session trial depends on regional infrastructure rollout speed and operator access policies.
Regulatory or operator restrictions on peak power allocation or on non‑OEM access could limit achievable peak power in some sites.

title: Contextual, AI-based cockpit assistant provides useful hands-free help and proactive suggestions
description: An in-cockpit assistant understands natural requests and proactively suggests contextual actions (navigation shortcuts, calendar-aware routing, media suggestions) so customers can get useful help hands-free and with fewer manual steps.
acceptance_criterion: Customer trial (field pilot): 100 representative EU users (owners or regular drivers of premium sedans; balanced tech-savvy and non-tech-savvy) use the assistant over 4 weeks in daily driving. Success metric is assistant task completion rate without fallback to manual UI: at least 70% of valid assistant requests (intent-defined set) must be completed end-to-end by the assistant without requiring the driver to use the touchscreen. Additionally, compared with a control group of 100 matched users in vehicles without the assistant, the trial group must report a statistically significant increase (p < 0.05) in perceived cockpit usefulness (measured by a validated 10-point scale) of ≥ 1.0 points. Pilot must log request types, success/failure reasons, and perceived usefulness.

reach.explanation: 2 of at most 40 mentions (square root scale); EU = 40 % of 2030 volume (127,000 cars)

competitive_pressure.explanation: no trusted web source shows a competitor advantage

future_relevance.explanation: linked to a 3-5 year trend (assumption); market growth 2025-2030: +10.4 %

rationale: Ranked mainly because of future relevance (10 points) and customer pain (7.5 points). Evidence level D: Bet on the next generation: only 0 direct customer mentions, the rest rests on trends (assumption).
assumptions: Cloud connectivity and edge compute available to support natural-language processing for the pilot; fallback handling is implemented safely.
Appropriate data-consent flows are in place so users agree to assistant telemetry for evaluation.
OEM backend and update channels support delivering incremental assistant improvements during the 4-week pilot.

title: Offer limited, regulated hands‑off driving on approved roads under strict conditions (pilot target)
description: On approved segments and under defined conditions, drivers can temporarily hand off lateral and longitudinal control to the vehicle for an extended, comfortable stretch (the vehicle clearly indicates when hands‑off is permitted and when the driver must resume control).
acceptance_criterion: Country‑by‑country pilot with N=50 consenting participants on approved routes where limited hands‑off operation is permitted. During the pilot measure total pilot kilometers and the proportion of kilometers where the system maintained lane position and speed without requiring corrective driver intervention. Pass if the system completes >=95% of pilot kilometers without safety‑critical interventions and participants report at least 80% perceived confidence/trust (measured via a post‑trial questionnaire). Document any driver takeover events and their causes. The pilot must run only where local approvals and regulations allow the tested functionality.
